items.body:
## Summary

A gateway async delegation dispatched before context compression can finish after the parent rotates to its compression-continuation child. The completion is then intentionally dropped by the #55578 fail-closed guard, even though the conversation is still live, and the durable row is marked `delivered`. No retry or restart recovery can surface it.

This is a distinct regression/edge case in the #55578 lifecycle hardening: explicit `/new` boundaries must remain fail-closed, but `end_reason=compression` is a continuation boundary, not a user-ended conversation.

## Confirmed production timeline

- delegation dispatched: 2026-07-16 11:08:29 local
- owning parent session compressed/ended: 2026-07-16 11:09:33
- continuation child started: 2026-07-16 11:09:33
- delegation completed: 2026-07-16 11:13:57
- gateway warning: `Async-delegation completion pinned to session ..., which is ended — dropping injection instead of resurrecting it (#55578 fail-closed)`
- durable record immediately became `delivery_state=delivered`, `delivery_attempts=1`
- no completion turn was injected into the live continuation; the result was found later only by manually inspecting the durable summary/cache

Environment: Hermes v0.18.2, macOS gateway/Telegram. The same guard is still present on current `origin/main` (`6cd5a2c5` at investigation time).

## Root cause

1. `_inject_watch_notification()` pins the synthetic event to `parent_session_id`.
2. `_handle_message_with_agent()` sees that the parent row has `ended_at` and drops it without checking `end_reason` or `get_compression_tip()`.
3. `BasePlatformAdapter.handle_message()` returns after scheduling background handling, so `_inject_watch_notification()` reports adapter acceptance before the inner handler has accepted the turn.
4. `_deliver_completion_notification()` therefore calls `complete_completion_delivery()` and marks the durable record delivered even though the inner handler dropped it.
5. Restart recovery only restores `delivery_state=pending`, so the false delivered state disables self-healing.

## Existing self-healing that does not cover this

- durable pending completion restoration
- exclusive claim/release/retry
- session-store and topic-binding compression-tip healing

The gateway pinning path bypasses compression-tip healing, and adapter acceptance is not an end-to-end delivery acknowledgement.

## Reproduction invariant

1. Start a gateway conversation.
2. Dispatch a `delegate_task` that outlives the current context window.
3. Trigger context compression before the child completes.
4. Let the child complete.
5. Assert the completion is injected into the live compression tip and the durable record is acknowledged only after that route accepts it.

Current behavior drops the completion and marks it delivered.

## Suggested narrow fix

Before applying the dead-session guard:

- if the pinned row is live, use it;
- if it ended for `compression`, resolve `get_compression_tip(parent)` and accept only a live continuation tip;
- for `/new`, reset, orphan reap, missing rows, or an ended tip, continue to fail closed;
- add a regression test where a compression parent resolves to a live child, plus a security assertion that explicit reset still drops.

A local TDD patch implementing that narrow distinction passes 86 relevant gateway tests (22 delegation/delivery + 64 session/topic-routing), `py_compile`, and `git diff --check`.

## Historical evidence

Retained gateway logs contain five occurrences of this exact ended-parent drop pattern between 2026-07-15 17:31 and 2026-07-16 11:13. Session rows for those incidents show compression-ended parents with continuation children, so this was not a one-off.

items.title: Bug: OpenRouter missing from PROVIDER_REGISTRY — desktop model picker drops it even with OPENROUTER_API_KEY set

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary
With a valid `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env`, OpenRouter works fine on the CLI (`hermes model`, `/model openrouter:...`), but it **does not appear as a selectable provider in the desktop app's model/provider picker**.

Root cause: `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` in `hermes_cli/auth.py` — the hand-maintained dict that `is_provider_explicitly_configured()` consults — has **no `openrouter` entry**. Every other provider is listed there, but OpenRouter was never added.

## Reproduction
1. Put a real key in `~/.hermes/.env`: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-...`
2. Open the desktop app -> model/provider picker (status bar / model menu).
3. Only `nous` (or whatever `model.provider` is set to) shows. OpenRouter is absent.

`hermes model` *does* list OpenRouter because it uses a different code path (`list_available_providers`, which reads `CANONICAL_PROVIDERS` and checks `os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")` directly, not `PROVIDER_REGISTRY`). So the behavior diverges between CLI and desktop.

## Why it's gated out
The desktop chat picker calls `GET /api/model/options?explicit_only=true` -> `inventory.build_models_payload(explicit_only=True)` -> `auth.is_provider_explicitly_configured("openrouter")`. That function's env-var check is:

```python
pconfig = PROVIDER_REGISTRY.get(normalized)   # normalized == "openrouter"
if pconfig and pconfig.auth_type == "api_key":
    for env_var in pconfig.api_key_env_vars:
        ...
```

`PROVIDER_REGISTRY.get("openrouter")` returns `None`, so check #3 is skipped and the function returns `False`. The picker then drops the `openrouter` row. `list_authenticated_providers()` *does* emit `openrouter` (it detects the key independently), so the row exists — it's only the `explicit_only` gate that removes it.

## Minimal fix
Add the missing entry to `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` in `hermes_cli/auth.py` (mirrors sibling `api_key` providers like `deepseek`/`anthropic`):

```python
"openrouter": ProviderConfig(
    id="openrouter",
    name="OpenRouter",
    auth_type="api_key",
    inference_base_url=OPENROUTER_BASE_URL,
    api_key_env_vars=("OPENROUTER_API_KEY",),
    base_url_env_var="OPENROUTER_BASE_URL",
),
```

`OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` is already imported in `auth.py` (`from hermes_constants import OPENROUTER_BASE_URL`).

## Verification
- `is_provider_explicitly_configured("openrouter")` returns `True` after the fix (was `False`); `nous` still `True`.
- `build_models_payload(explicit_only=True)` payload now includes both `nous` and `openrouter` (was just `nous`).
- `bash scripts/run_tests.sh tests/hermes_cli/test_inventory.py tests/hermes_cli/test_auth_provider_gate.py tests/hermes_cli/test_list_picker_providers.py tests/hermes_cli/test_api_key_providers.py tests/hermes_cli/test_configured_builtin_models.py` -> **249 passed, 0 failed**.
- Confirmed the bug is present on `origin/main` (no `openrouter` key in `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` there either; gate logic identical).

## Environment
- hermes-agent 0.18.2 (`_config_version: 33`)
- Local HEAD: `23526148` "fix(terminal): bridge terminal.backend config in serve/desktop processes..."
- macOS 26.5.2 (desktop app: `apps/desktop/release/mac-arm64/Hermes.app`)
- `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` = `sk-or-v1-...` (valid, confirmed active)

## Affected users
Anyone who set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` but did *not* also set `model.provider: openrouter` in config.yaml — they correctly expect OpenRouter to show up as a configured provider in the GUI, but it silently doesn't.

## Bug Report

### Summary
After updating Hermes, the active model in the desktop app drifts to a different model/provider than what is pinned in `config.yaml`. In this case, config has `model.provider: custom:<provider>` and `model.default: minimax-m2.7`, but the desktop UI showed `llama3.1:8b-instruct-q8_0` (an Ollama/LM Studio model) and returned `404` errors when sending messages.

### Environment
- **OS:** Windows 10 (AMD Ryzen 5 5600G, 16GB RAM, no CUDA GPU)
- **Hermes version:** Latest (config_version: 33)
- **Provider config:** `custom_providers` with MaxPlus (Chinese API gateway), LM Studio, Ollama, and llama.cpp providers

### Config (relevant sections)
```yaml
model:
  provider: custom:โมเดลจีน      # pinned to MaxPlus
  default: minimax-m2.7            # pinned model

moa:
  enabled: true                    # MOA was enabled
  reference_models:
    - provider: openai-codex
      model: gpt-5.5
    - provider: openrouter
      model: deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
  aggregator:
    provider: openrouter
      model: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8

auxiliary:
  vision:
    provider: auto                 # auto-routing
  web_extract:
    provider: auto
  compression:
    provider: auto
```

### What happened
1. `config.yaml` explicitly pins `model.provider` and `model.default` to a cloud provider
2. After a Hermes update, the desktop app's model selector showed `llama3.1:8b-instruct-q8_0` instead
3. Sending "hello" returned `{"error": "Request failed: 404"}` — the local model wasn't actually running
4. User had to manually re-select the correct model from the dropdown

### Suspected causes
1. **MOA routing override** — With `moa.enabled: true`, MOA may route requests to reference models or auxiliary providers that override the pinned `model.default`. If a reference model isn't available, it may fall back to a local provider (Ollama/LM Studio) without user consent.
2. **`auxiliary.*.provider: auto`** — Auto-detection may pick up local providers (LM Studio at `:1234`, Ollama at `:11434`) and override the main chat lane when the desktop app restores session state.
3. **Desktop app localStorage** — The Electron frontend may cache the last-selected model from a previous session and override `config.yaml` settings on startup.
4. **Update process** — `hermes update` may reset or shuffle provider/model selection during config migration.

### Expected behavior
- `model.provider` and `model.default` in `config.yaml` should be the **authoritative source** for the active model
- MOA and auxiliary providers should not override the main chat lane
- After updates, the pinned model should persist

### Workaround
- Manually re-select the model from the dropdown (`/model custom:<provider>/<model>`)
- Disable MOA (`moa.enabled: false`) if not actively using mixture-of-agents

### Impact
- **Severity:** Medium — causes confusion and broken sessions after updates
- **Frequency:** Recurring (happened multiple times across different update cycles)
- **User profile:** Non-programmer user on constrained hardware with multiple local + cloud providers configured

## Summary

Hermes Desktop can crash immediately after an update because Vite resolves an untracked JavaScript sibling in `apps/desktop/src/lib/` instead of the tracked TypeScript implementation. The stale file calls a removed assistant-ui repository API.

## Environment

- Hermes Desktop 0.17.0
- macOS arm64
- Source revision: `6cd5a2c5f7baf2ae45d22183d11614d1f0301c89`

## Reproduction

1. Have both files present:
   - `apps/desktop/src/lib/incremental-external-store-runtime.ts`
   - untracked `apps/desktop/src/lib/incremental-external-store-runtime.js`
2. Build Desktop with `npm run build` from `apps/desktop`.
3. Launch the packaged desktop app.

## Actual behavior

The renderer repeatedly enters the root error boundary:

```text
TypeError: this.repository.appendOptimisticMessage is not a function
```

The stale `.js` file contains the obsolete `appendOptimisticMessage(...)` call. The tracked `.ts` version correctly uses `addOrUpdateMessage(...)`, but the bare import `@/lib/incremental-external-store-runtime` resolves to the `.js` sibling during the build. The result is packaged into the renderer bundle.

## Expected behavior

The desktop build should package the tracked TypeScript runtime and launch without the root renderer crash.

## Suggested fix

- Ensure install/update/build flows never emit or retain generated `.js` files under `apps/desktop/src/`.
- Add a packaging regression test that fails when a `.js` sibling shadows a `.ts` source module, or assert the production bundle does not contain `appendOptimisticMessage`.
- Consider making Vite resolution prefer TypeScript extensions for source imports, though removing generated source-tree artifacts is the primary fix.

## Verification after local repair

Deleting the untracked `.js` sibling and rebuilding produced a new bundle containing `addOrUpdateMessage` and no `appendOptimisticMessage` references.

## Bug description

While CLI voice mode is active, user messages are presented to the agent with a `[Voice input]` marker even when the user intentionally typed the message rather than recording audio. The model therefore cannot reliably distinguish actual speech-to-text output from typed input.

This caused the agent to treat a typed troubleshooting message as evidence that transcription had begun working correctly, despite the user clarifying that it had not been transcribed.

1. Start Hermes CLI and enable voice mode.
2. Send an actual recorded voice message.

Both messages are marked `[Voice input]`, so the marker appears to describe the active mode or input channel rather than the provenance of the individual message.

Only messages actually produced by speech-to-text should be identified as transcribed voice input. Typed messages should remain unmarked, or each message should carry explicit provenance such as `input_source: typed` versus `input_source: voice_transcription`.

This distinction would let the agent recognize likely transcription failures, call out garbled text, and avoid treating manually typed follow-ups as successful STT output.

items.title: [Bug]: dashboard console skills commands act on the wrong profile — tools/skills_sync.py binds SKILLS_DIR at import and _profile_scope doesn't retarget it

items.body:
`hermes_cli/web_server.py:13566` `_profile_scope()` documents this exact bug class, and fixes it for two modules:

> 2. `tools.skills_tool` and `tools.skill_manager_tool` bind `SKILLS_DIR` at import time, so the override CANNOT reach them. Like `_call_cron_for_profile` does for cron's module globals, temporarily retarget both under a lock and restore them immediately after.

`tools/skills_sync.py:39-41` has the identical import-time binding and is **not** retargeted.

## The chain

1. `_execute_console_line()` (`web_server.py:15489`) wraps dashboard console dispatch in `with _profile_scope(profile):`, which calls `set_hermes_home_override(profile_dir)` and retargets only `skills_tool` + `skill_manager_tool`.
2. `("skills","reset")`, `("skills","diff")`, `("skills","list-modified")`, `("skills","opt-in")`, `("skills","opt-out")`, `("skills","repair-official")` are console-allowed (`console_engine.py:194-208`) and dispatch **in-process** — unlike hub `install`/`update`/`uninstall`, which correctly go through a fresh profile-scoped subprocess (`web_server.py:12501`).
3. `hermes_cli/skills_hub.py` lazily imports from `tools.skills_sync`: `reset_bundled_skill` (:1152), `list_user_modified_bundled_skills` (:1195), `diff_bundled_skill` (:1222), `sync_skills`/`set_bundled_skills_opt_out` (:1337), `restore_official_optional_skill` (:1365).
4. Those functions read the frozen module constants: `MANIFEST_FILE` (:104), `SKILLS_DIR` (:307, :340, :744), `HERMES_HOME` (:496, :1052).

So `skills_sync` binds to whichever profile first triggered a console skills command, and every later console skills op under a different profile resolves against that stale home.

## Why this one bites harder than its two siblings

`reset_bundled_skill()` **deletes**, and its safety boundary is the frozen constant. `skills_sync.py:744` does `skills_root = SKILLS_DIR.resolve()`, which backs the strict-child check whose own comment says it exists so a collapsed `dest` can't "wipe every installed skill". Under a mismatched profile that guard is computed against the wrong root.

## Precedent — this is the third module in the same lineage

- `f8723c478` — fix(skills): resolve skills dir from active profile → `tools/skills_tool.py`
- `c6a3d412d` — fix(skills): widen call-time skills-dir resolution to `skill_manager_tool` (refs #40677)
- `tools/skills_sync.py` — same binding, still unfixed

The pattern to copy exists in both: keep the module attribute, snapshot `_SKILLS_DIR_AT_IMPORT`, add a call-time accessor that honors an explicit monkeypatch (`configured != _AT_IMPORT`) and otherwise re-resolves live.

`hermes_cli/profiles.py:1186` (`seed_profile_skills`: *"Uses subprocess because sync_skills() caches HERMES_HOME at module level"*) shows the caching is already known — but that workaround only covers profile seeding, not the console path.

## Note on AGENTS.md:1193

> "Module-level constants are fine — they cache `get_hermes_home()` at import time, which is AFTER `_apply_profile_override()` sets the env var."

That holds for the one-shot CLI, but not for the `set_hermes_home_override()` ContextVar used by long-lived processes — which is the very seam `_profile_scope` exists to paper over. Worth correcting, or it keeps inviting this class of bug.

## Scope — correcting my original filing

I first filed this as a repo-wide sweep of module-level `get_hermes_home()` captures. **That was wrong and I've narrowed it.** Most such captures are harmless: one-shot CLI processes, constants consumed one line later, dead constants (e.g. `tools/file_operations.py:49-53` — `WRITE_DENIED_PATHS`/`WRITE_DENIED_PREFIXES` have no readers at all; the live guard `agent/file_safety.py:97-103` re-resolves per call), or daemon state that *should* anchor to the launch home. At least one — `cron/jobs.py:66` — is a deliberate, documented compatibility fallback with `use_cron_store()` as the sanctioned call-time seam; converting it would contradict the maintainers' stated intent. Each site needs its own demonstrated post-override consumer, so I'm not proposing a blanket sweep.

One other site looks real on the same evidence standard: `hermes_state.py:141` `DEFAULT_DB_PATH`, read via `SessionDB()` in `cron/scheduler.py:2732`/`2740` under the dashboard's `_fire_cron_job_for_profile` override (`web_server.py:10879`), and in `console_engine.py`'s `SessionDB()` sites under `_profile_scope`. Happy to split that into its own issue rather than widen this one.

PR for `skills_sync` only to follow.

Body:

Environment
Windows 10
Hermes Desktop v0.1.82 (+17)
Provider: moa (Mixture of Agents preset-based routing)
Model: Custom Chinese preset names (e.g., 日常对话-高峰, 日常对话-非高峰)
Summary
When creating a new conversation in the Hermes desktop app, the session appears in the sidebar and the composer shows as "waiting," but the agent never responds. No visible error is shown to the user — the conversation simply hangs indefinitely with no feedback. Existing conversations may also suddenly stop responding.

Root Cause Analysis
From examining agent.log, errors.log, and desktop.log, two distinct crash patterns are responsible:

1. MoA Preset KeyError — Mismatched preset name
ERROR [20260715_181609_b8ba74] agent.conversation_loop: API call failed after 3 retries. '日常对话-高峰期' | provider=moa model=日常对话-高峰期 msgs=12 tokens=~9,503

The session is attempting to use the preset name 日常对话-高峰期 (with 期 character), but moa.presets in config.yaml only defines 日常对话-高峰 (without 期) and 日常对话-非高峰. The extra 期 causes a KeyError in the MoA preset lookup — the preset name literally does not exist in the configuration dictionary.

How this happens:

The user's config.yaml defines moa.presets.日常对话-高峰 and model.default: 日常对话-高峰
But the session's stored model name is 日常对话-高峰期
This likely originates from a config drift: either a previous version of the config had 高峰期 as the naming convention, or a different config entry uses 高峰期 while the moa.presets section uses 高峰
When MoA calls moa_config.get_preset("日常对话-高峰期"), it raises KeyError
Log evidence: 2026-07-17 01:44:48,906 WARNING agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 1/3) error_type=KeyError provider=moa model=日常对话-高峰期 summary='日常对话-高峰期'

2026-07-17 01:44:56,374 WARNING agent.chat_completion_helpers: Fallback to moa failed: provider not configured (repeated 3 times)

2026-07-17 01:44:56,394 ERROR agent.conversation_loop: API call failed after 3 retries. '日常对话-高峰期' | provider=moa model=日常对话-高峰期 msgs=12 tokens=~9,503

After 3 retries plus 3 fallback attempts, the session is dead — but the UI shows no error. The desktop.log confirms:

[hermes] ⚠️ API call failed (attempt 1/3): KeyError [hermes] 🔌 Provider: moa Model: 日常对话-高峰期 [hermes] ❌ API failed after 3 retries — '日常对话-高峰期' [hermes] 💀 Final error: '日常对话-高峰期'

### 2. OverflowError — Token budget calculation yields infinity

WARNING agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 1/3) error_type=OverflowError provider=moa model=日常对话-非高峰 summary=cannot convert float infinity to integer

Even when the preset name is correct, MoA sessions with a long context (~127k tokens, 183 messages) crash with `OverflowError: cannot convert float infinity to integer`. This suggests a division-by-zero or uninitialized float value in the token budget calculation path — likely in the `max_tokens` or `max_iterations` budget computation when token counts approach model limits.

2026-07-16 18:32:45,934 ERROR agent.conversation_loop: API call failed after 3 retries. cannot convert float infinity to integer | provider=moa model=日常对话-非高峰 msgs=183 tokens=~127,939


### 3. Secondary issues compounding the problem

**a) Mem0 backend permanently broken (OSS mode):**

ERROR plugins.memory.mem0: Mem0 backend failed to initialize (oss mode): BaseEmbedderConfig.init() got an unexpected keyword argument 'api_base'

This fires on every agent init (~30+ times in recent logs). Mem0's OSS mode has an API incompatibility with the installed version.

**b) MiniMax-CN insufficient balance:**

WARNING agent.auxiliary_client: Auxiliary: marking minimax-cn unhealthy for 600s (payment / credit error). Error code: 402 - insufficient balance (1008)

The MiniMax M3 reference model used in MoA presets (日常对话-非高峰, 日常对话-高峰, etc.) has no credit balance, causing MoA reference calls to fail. While MoA has fallback logic, this adds latency and may exhaust fallbacks.

## Desktop-Side Impact

1. **No user-facing error:** When the API call fails after retries, the desktop UI simply shows "thinking..." indefinitely or returns to idle with no response. The user has no way to know the conversation is dead.

2. **Session appears in sidebar but is non-functional:** The session list entry is created, but the agent runtime has already failed internally. Clicking it shows an empty or stuck thread.

3. **No retry mechanism in the UI:** After a silent failure, there is no "Retry" button or error banner in the chat view. The user must manually create a `/new` session, which may hit the same error.

## Suggested Fixes

1. **Graceful preset resolution:** When a MoA preset name doesn't match, fall back to `moa.default_preset` instead of raising KeyError. Surface a visible warning to the user that the requested preset was not found.

2. **OverflowError guard:** Add a try/except or input validation in the token budget calculation path to prevent `float('inf')` from reaching `int()` conversion. Validate max_tokens / budget values before passing to the API.

3. **Desktop error surface:** When an API call fails after all retries, the desktop UI should show an error banner with the error message (not just "thinking..." forever). Add a retry button in the conversation view.

4. **Mem0 compatibility fix:** Update the Mem0 plugin's config to not pass `api_base` if the installed Mem0 version doesn't support it, or pin a compatible Mem0 version.

5. **Preset name validation on config load:** When loading MoA presets, validate that `model.default` is a key that exists in `moa.presets`. If not, print a clear warning.

## Workaround

1. Check `moa.presets` in `config.yaml` and ensure the preset name in `model.default` matches exactly.
2. Remove trailing/debounced preset names like `高峰期` vs `高峰`.
3. Ensure MiniMax account has sufficient balance if using it as a reference model.
4. Restart Hermes desktop after fixing config.

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state

items.body: Environment Hermes Desktop v0.1.82 (+17) Provider: moa Any provider supporting /model mid-session switching Summary Every time a user switches models mid-session via /model, a system marker is injected into the conversation history as a user-role message. These markers accumulate permanently, consuming context window tokens on every subsequent API call. After several model switches, hundreds of tokens are wasted per turn — and these markers survive context compression. Evidence User screenshot 1: 5 consecutive model switch markers [System: The active model for this chat has changed to 质量-非高峰 via provider moa. ...] [System: The active model for this chat has changed to 省钱-非高峰 via provider moa. ...] [System: The active model for this chat has changed to 代码编程-非高峰 via provider moa. ...] [System: The active model for this chat has changed to 日常对话-非高峰 via provider moa. ...] [System: The active model for this chat has changed to 智能-高峰 via provider moa. ...] ### Token cost per marker Each marker is ~210 bytes. In mixed Chinese+English, that's approximately 80–120 tokens per marker. Five switches = ~400–600 tokens permanently consumed from the context window on every single API call. ### Comment on the same root cause — observed as two different symptoms: In short: Issue A = images appear without adding them. Issue B = images reappear after clicking ✕. Both stem from the same root cause — the composer-images\ directory has no cleanup mechanism, and the ✕ button only performs a UI-level removal without deleting the underlying file. Suggestion for the fix: The ✕ (remove) action should either (a) delete the corresponding .png cache file, or (b) the attachment picker should not source its items from a global persistent directory at all — only from the current session's actual attachments. ## Root Cause — Source Code **File:** `tui_gateway/server.py` (line 2445–2478) ```python def _append_model_switch_marker(session, *, model, provider): marker = ( "[System: The active model for this chat has changed to " f"{model}{provider_part}. From this point forward, use this runtime " "metadata when answering questions about what model/provider is active.]" ) # Persist as a user message, not a system message. The gateway appends # this marker after prior conversation turns, and strict OpenAI-compatible # providers (vLLM, Qwen) reject system messages that are not at the # beginning of the API message list (#48338). entry = {"role": "user", "content": marker} session.setdefault("history", []).append(entry) ... db.append_message(session_id=session_key, role="user", content=marker) Called at line 3011: _append_model_switch_marker( session, model=result.new_model, provider=result.target_provider ) ### Why it's wasteful 1. **Every `/model` switch adds a permanent marker** — each is ~80–120 tokens as a `user` message. Switching models 10 times = ~1000 tokens burned on metadata. 2. **Markers survive context compression** — because they are stored as `user`-role messages (not system), the compression algorithm treats them as legitimate conversation history and preserves them. They cannot be pruned without losing the actual conversation context around them. 3. **Redundant with existing metadata** — the active model/provider is already available through: - `session.info` events emitted to the desktop UI - Agent internal state (`agent.model`, `agent.provider`) - The status bar model pill - The `model` field in every API call response The agent does not need to re-read its own model name from a conversation message. 4. **Self-referential compounding** — if a user switches models to investigate a model-switching bug, each diagnostic switch adds MORE markers, consuming the very context tokens needed to debug the issue. 5. **No opt-out or cleanup** — there is no config flag to disable these markers, no TTL, and no mechanism to clear them even when the model stabilizes. ## Desktop Impact 1. **Unnecessary token cost** — each model switch permanently reduces the effective context window. For users who frequently switch MoA presets to compare behavior, this compounds rapidly. 2. **Context pollution** — the conversation history becomes cluttered with "[System: ...]" messages that the user didn't write and didn't ask for. 3. **User confusion** — users see these messages and ask "why are these here?" or "did I send these?" as shown in the attached screenshots. 4. **Compression inefficiency** — context compression must preserve these markers along with real conversation turns, reducing compression effectiveness. ## Suggested Fixes 1. **Store as agent-side metadata instead of conversation messages** — the model switch info should be kept in the agent's runtime state (already present) and optionally surfaced through a separate metadata channel, not injected as a visible conversation message. 2. **Add a config flag** — e.g., `model.switch_marker: false` in config.yaml to suppress marker generation entirely. 3. **Make markers ephemeral** — if persisted, limit to the most recent marker only (replace on each switch) instead of appending. 4. **Compression-aware markers** — mark these entries as compressible so the context compressor can prune old markers when the context window is tight. 5. **Remove the marker altogether** — the agent already has accurate model/provider data through its initialization and `session.info` events. The marker serves no functional purpose that isn't already covered. ## Workaround Avoid switching models frequently in a single conversation. Use `/new` to start a fresh conversation with the desired model instead.

items.title: [Feature]: Disable persistent context-window caching for volatile provider catalogs

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Problem or use case

Hermes persists discovered context-window values indefinitely in `context_length_cache.yaml`, then checks that disk cache before provider-aware live resolution in `agent/model_metadata.py`.

That is unsafe for providers whose authenticated model catalog is dynamic and authoritative, especially `openai-codex` (`GET https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/models`). Provider rollouts, account entitlements, temporary rollbacks, and pricing/accounting changes can alter `context_window` without changing the model slug.

A real incident exposed two failure modes:

- GPT-5.6 Codex metadata was cached at `372000`; OpenAI later rolled the live route back to `272000` because the larger window caused more subscription usage to be charged than intended: https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2076495156757577895
- Hermes continued accepting the persisted `372000` value because the current Codex invalidation guard only drops cached values `>= 400000`. A previously valid `372000` value therefore remained trusted indefinitely.
- Exact URL keys also split the cache: `model@.../codex` could remain `372000` while `model@.../codex/` contained `272000`.
- Multi-profile installations amplify the problem because each profile can retain an independent stale cache file.

The general problem is not that one threshold is wrong. It is that value-based invalidation cannot safely determine whether provider-owned metadata is still current.

## Requested feature

Add a provider-level cache policy and treat live authenticated catalogs such as `openai-codex` as **volatile/live-first metadata**.

For `openai-codex` specifically:

1. Do not read context-window values from the persistent `context_length_cache.yaml`.
2. Do not write live Codex `/models` context values to that persistent cache.
3. Query the authenticated Codex model catalog on fresh process/session startup.
4. Keep the existing short in-memory TTL to avoid repeated network calls within one process.
5. If the live catalog is unavailable, use the bundled provider-specific catalog/fallback for that run, but do not persist the fallback or guess indefinitely.
6. Canonicalize base URLs before any cache keying (`rstrip("/")`, normalized scheme/host/path) so trailing-slash variants cannot diverge.
7. Preserve explicit user overrides, but expose that they are manual overrides rather than provider-advertised limits.

A generic policy could look conceptually like:

```python
PERSISTENT_CONTEXT_CACHE_POLICY = {
    "openai-codex": "disabled",   # live catalog + process-local TTL
    "nous": "live-reconcile",
    "local": "endpoint-specific",
    "default": "persistent",
}
```

The exact API is not important; the invariant is that dynamic provider metadata must not become an immortal disk fact.

## Why this should be a feature rather than another hardcoded invalidation rule

The current `cached >= 400_000` Codex guard fixes one historical failure mode but cannot handle valid provider transitions such as:

- `372000 -> 272000`
- account/plan-specific catalog changes
- model rollouts where the same slug changes in either direction
- any future value that does not cross a hardcoded threshold

Adding more model/value exceptions will keep failing whenever the provider changes a number Hermes did not anticipate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `openai-codex` context resolution ignores existing persistent context-cache entries.
- [ ] Live Codex `/models` results are not written to `context_length_cache.yaml`.
- [ ] A provider transition from `372000` to `272000` is picked up automatically by a fresh process/session without manual cache deletion.
- [ ] Existing stale Codex cache files become harmless without requiring a migration.
- [ ] Trailing-slash and normalized-equivalent URLs cannot resolve to different context windows.
- [ ] Live probe failures use a provider-specific fallback for the current run and do not persist it as authoritative metadata.
- [ ] `/model`, diagnostics, or logs can identify the context source: live catalog, bundled fallback, or explicit user override.
- [ ] Tests cover value changes in both directions, probe failure, URL normalization, and isolated multi-profile homes.

## Alternatives considered

### Persistent cache with a TTL

Better than the current indefinite cache, but still unnecessary for an authenticated endpoint that is already queried with a process-local TTL. If persistent caching is retained, entries need timestamps, strict expiration, canonical URL keys, source metadata, and live reconciliation before use.

### More value-based invalidation rules

Rejected. The 372K-to-272K incident demonstrates that a previously valid value can become stale without crossing a predictable threshold.

### Manual cache cleanup

Not acceptable as a normal operating requirement, particularly for multi-profile deployments. Users should not need to inspect and repair YAML metadata after provider-side rollouts.

## Relevant code

- `agent/model_metadata.py::save_context_length`
- `agent/model_metadata.py::get_cached_context_length`
- `agent/model_metadata.py::get_model_context_length`
- `agent/model_metadata.py::_fetch_codex_oauth_context_lengths`
- `agent/model_metadata.py::_resolve_codex_oauth_context_length`

Current ordering allows a persistent value to return before the live Codex provider branch, and the Codex branch writes its result back to persistent storage.

items.title: PYTHONPATH leaks to child processes, breaking pipx-installed CLI tools with C extension dependencies

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes sets `PYTHONPATH` as a global environment variable pointing to its own venv (`hermes-agent/venv/Lib/site-packages`). This `PYTHONPATH` is inherited by **all child processes** spawned via the `terminal` tool, breaking pipx-installed CLI tools that rely on C extension packages (Pillow, numpy, etc.).

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Hermes Agent: desktop app, Python 3.11 venv
- Affected tool: bili-cli (pipx, Python 3.13 venv)
- Also affects: any pipx CLI tool with C extension deps

## Reproduction

1. Install a pipx tool with C extension deps (e.g., `pipx install bilibili-cli`)
2. From a Hermes `terminal` call, run the tool directly:

```bash
bili search "test" --type video -n 1
```

3. Observe: the process hangs (appears as timeout) or crashes with `ImportError`.

## Root Cause

```bash
echo "PYTHONPATH=$PYTHONPATH"
# Output:
# C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent
# C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages
```

Python module search priority: `PYTHONPATH` > venv `site-packages`. So when bili-cli (Python 3.13) starts, it finds Pillow in Hermes's venv (Python 3.11) first, loads the `_imaging` C extension, and fails due to version mismatch:

```
ImportError: cannot import name '_imaging' from 'PIL' (C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\PIL\__init__.py)
```

The pipx venv isolation is effectively bypassed because `PYTHONPATH` overrides it.

## Diagnosis Steps

```bash
# With inherited PYTHONPATH - fails (loads PIL from Hermes venv)
/c/Users/<user>/pipx/venvs/bilibili-cli/Scripts/python.exe -c "from PIL import _imaging; print(\"OK\")"
# ImportError

# Without PYTHONPATH - works (loads PIL from pipx venv)
env -u PYTHONPATH /c/Users/<user>/pipx/venvs/bilibili-cli/Scripts/python.exe -c "from PIL import _imaging; print(\"OK\")"
# OK
```

## Impact

- Affects **all** pipx-installed CLI tools with C extension dependencies (Pillow, numpy, lxml, etc.)
- The failure mode (hang/timeout) is hard to diagnose — no obvious error message unless you trace imports
- Users must manually create wrapper scripts to strip `PYTHONPATH`, which is fragile and breaks on pipx upgrades

## Suggested Fix

Hermes should not leak its internal `PYTHONPATH` to child processes spawned via the `terminal` tool. Options:

1. **Unset `PYTHONPATH` when spawning terminal subprocesses** (simplest, most robust)
2. Use `sys.path.insert()` instead of `PYTHONPATH` env var for internal Python imports (keeps it in-process only)
3. Only inject `PYTHONPATH` for `execute_code` calls, not for `terminal` tool calls

## Current Workaround

Create a bash wrapper in `~/.local/bin/` that strips `PYTHONPATH` and calls the tool's own venv Python directly:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
exec env -u PYTHONPATH /c/Users/<user>/pipx/venvs/bilibili-cli/Scripts/python.exe -m bili_cli.cli "$@"
```

Note: A wrapper named `bili` is shadowed by `bili.exe` on Windows (PE binaries take priority over extensionless scripts in PATH resolution), so the wrapper must bypass the `.exe` entry point entirely.

items.title: [Bug]: Retry can supersede a still-live SSE stream without aborting it — two streams interleave token-by-token into one transcript turn

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

When stream recovery issues a retry while the prior SSE stream is still
delivering (observed via the stale-stream / reconnect path), the superseded
stream is not positively terminated: both the old and the new stream write
deltas into the same turn, and the persisted transcript for that turn is two
coherent responses interleaved word-by-word / token-by-token.

Downstream we root-caused two "garbled model output" reports to exactly this:
de-interleaving the stored text by alternation yields two complete, fluent,
independently coherent answers to the same prompt. That signature rules out
model/context failure — it is a dual-writer race in the harness.

## Where we think it lives

`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`, `interruptible_streaming_api_call()`:

- The interrupt path sets `_request_cancelled["value"] = True` **before**
  force-closing, so the worker recognizes its own forced close and exits
  (the #6600 fix). The **stale-kill path does not** — it only calls
  `_close_request_client_once("stale_stream_kill")` and resets the timer.
  The superseded worker's death is therefore only as reliable as the socket
  abort, and `request_client_holder` can be swapped by the worker between
  attempts, so the abort can miss the live stream entirely.
- Once a retry attempt starts, nothing fences the old attempt out of the
  delta sink: any late chunks from the superseded stream still flow through
  `agent._fire_stream_delta` / `_current_streamed_assistant_text` alongside
  the new attempt's chunks.

Related but distinct: #64934 documents the same single-writer-invariant
violation on the transcript when two *turns* overlap; this report is the
retry-supersession variant within one turn. Also adjacent: #58962, #53449.

## Expected

Exactly one stream may write to a turn. A retry must first hard-abort the
superseded stream (cancellation token checked in the delta path, not just a
socket abort), and only then begin streaming.

## Proposed acceptance criteria

- [ ] A retry issued while a stream is live aborts the superseded stream;
      the transcript records exactly one response for the turn (guard the
      delta sink by attempt id, not only by socket state).
- [ ] The aborted stream is logged (turn id, attempt id, bytes/chunks
      discarded) — silent discard would hide real provider failures.
- [ ] Regression test simulates the race (two attempt streams feeding one
      turn) and asserts single-writer output.

## Environment

hermes-agent v0.18.0 (native install via hermes-agent.nousresearch.com
install.sh), Linux VPS. Happy to supply the de-interleaved transcript
forensics on request.

File created at `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` as reported.

File created at `skills/.archive/<name>/SKILL.md`. Reported path is incorrect.

`skill_manager_tool.py` `_create_skill()` (lines 793-858) calls `_resolve_skill_dir()` (line 578) which returns `_skills_dir() / category / name`. There is NO reference to `.archive` anywhere in the create path. `_atomic_write_text()` writes to the given path without redirection.

Use `write_file` directly to the expected path under `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md`.

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

items.body:
## Summary
In Hermes Desktop, clicking **Read aloud** on a longer assistant reply fails with:

> **Read aloud failed** — Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms

Short replies read aloud fine; only replies whose TTS takes more than ~15s to synthesize fail. This looks like a regression introduced with the recent auto-speak / read-aloud work.

## Environment
- Hermes Desktop **0.17.0** (macOS, Apple Silicon)
- TTS provider: `xai` (voice `ara`)
- Backend: local Hermes gateway

## Steps to reproduce
1. Set the TTS provider to xAI (`ara`) in `config.yaml`.
2. Get a long assistant reply (long enough that speech synthesis takes >15s).
3. Click **Read aloud**.
4. After 15s: *"Read aloud failed — Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms."*

## Expected vs. actual
- **Expected:** Read aloud waits long enough for the audio to synthesize (the backend's own xAI TTS request already allows 60s).
- **Actual:** The desktop client aborts the request at 15s, before the audio returns.

## Root cause (from the source)
The read-aloud request uses the app's **generic default fetch timeout**, not a TTS-appropriate one:

- `apps/desktop/electron/hardening.ts`: `const DEFAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`
- The read-aloud fetch resolves its timeout via `resolveTimeoutMs(options.timeoutMs, DEFAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)` and passes no explicit value, so it falls back to 15s.
- `resolveTimeoutMs` reads **no environment or config override** — only an explicit per-call value or the 15s fallback. So there's no user-side setting to work around it.

## Why this looks like a regression
The auto-speak / read-aloud feature and its wiring to the generic 15s fetch timeout are all recent (roughly late June – mid July 2026): the auto-speak watcher hook, the `useComposerVoice` engine extraction, the TypeScript refactor that introduced `DEFAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`, and the chat-view/composer integration. The failures began right after these landed.

## Suggested fix
Give the TTS / read-aloud fetch path its own timeout, well above the backend's TTS ceiling:
- Pass an explicit `timeoutMs` (e.g. **60–120s**) on the read-aloud request, **or**
- Make the default configurable via env/setting (e.g. `HERMES_DESKTOP_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`).

The backend's xAI TTS request already allows 60s (`tools/tts_tool.py` → `_generate_xai_tts`, `timeout=60`), so the desktop client should wait at least that long for the read-aloud response.

## Note on local workarounds
There's no practical user-side workaround: the value is compiled into the packaged app, and the shipped `app.asar` is integrity-protected (`ElectronAsarIntegrity` in `Info.plist`), so patching the built bundle isn't viable without rebuilding and re-signing. A fix in the app itself is needed.

items.title: hermes -z (oneshot) silently ignores terminal.backend and executes tools with the local backend — sandbox bypass

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
### Summary

`hermes -z` (oneshot) **silently ignores `terminal.backend`** and runs every terminal-tool call with the **local** backend, in-process, regardless of what the user configured. A user who set `terminal.backend: ssh` (or `docker`/`daytona`/`modal`) specifically to sandbox tool execution gets oneshot commands executed **directly in the host/container environment with no warning and no error** — the isolation they configured is silently bypassed.

This is the security-relevant sibling of the terminal-config-bridge issues already tracked (#28892 bridge drift, #29239 "config.yaml authoritative for terminal.backend", #61882 "fail closed when the bridge is unavailable"): those cover the bridge being *wrong* or *unavailable*; this is the bridge being **never invoked at all** on the oneshot path, which fails **open** to local.

### Environment

- Hermes Agent **v0.18.2** (`2026.7.7.2`, upstream `bb5fc723`)
- Python 3.11.15, Linux (Fedora), podman container
- `config.yaml`: `terminal.backend: ssh` (tool execution meant to run in an isolated SSH sandbox VM)
- Confirmed still present on `main`: `hermes_cli/oneshot.py` contains **no** `TERMINAL_ENV` / config-bridge reference, and `hermes_cli/main.py` dispatches oneshot via `_prepare_agent_startup(args)` → `run_oneshot(...)`, neither of which applies the terminal bridge.

### Root cause

The config→env bridge that maps `terminal.backend` to `TERMINAL_ENV` (which `tools/terminal_tool.py` actually reads — it defaults to `"local"` when the var is unset) lives in **two** places, and **both are on paths the oneshot never takes**:

- `cli.py` `load_cli_config()` — runs at `import cli` (`CLI_CONFIG = load_cli_config()`), i.e. the interactive CLI/TUI path.
- `gateway/run.py` — the gateway's own bridge block.

The oneshot dispatch (`main.py`: `if getattr(args, "oneshot", ...)` → `_prepare_agent_startup(args)` → `run_oneshot()`) **bypasses `cli.py` entirely** (as `oneshot.py`'s own docstring states: *"Bypasses cli.py entirely."*) and does not run the gateway bridge either. So `TERMINAL_ENV` is never set from config, `terminal_tool` sees it empty, and falls back to `local`.

### Reproduction

With `terminal.backend: ssh` configured and working (verified below), from inside the same container:

**1. Oneshot — reads empty `TERMINAL_ENV`, runs locally:**
```console
$ hermes -z "Run with the terminal tool: cat /etc/hostname; echo USER=$(whoami); echo TERMINAL_ENV=$TERMINAL_ENV — reply with only the raw output."
4ceb3b8ccccb          # <-- the hermes container's own hostname
USER=hermes           # <-- the container user, NOT the sandbox
TERMINAL_ENV=         # <-- empty: the bridge never ran
```

**2. Same container, with the bridge applied (`import cli` runs `load_cli_config()`) — routes to the SSH sandbox as configured:**
```console
$ python -c "import cli; from tools.terminal_tool import terminal_tool; print(terminal_tool('hostname && whoami'))"
{"output": "fedora\nsandbox", "exit_code": 0, "error": null}   # <-- the sandbox VM
```

Identical config, identical command, opposite execution environment — the only difference is whether the terminal bridge ran. Oneshot is the branch where it doesn't.

### Impact

- **Sandbox bypass (security):** the entire point of a non-local `terminal.backend` is to keep model-driven shell execution off the host. Oneshot defeats that silently. `hermes -z` is exactly the mode people wire into scripts, cron, and CI — unattended contexts where a silent fallback to local execution is worst-case.
- **Silent, not fail-loud:** no warning, no error, exit code 0. The user has no signal that isolation was dropped.
- **Consistency:** interactive chat, TUI, and gateway sessions all honor `terminal.backend`; only oneshot doesn't, so the same config behaves differently depending on entry point.

### Suggested direction

Apply the terminal config bridge on the oneshot path before the agent runs — ideally by extracting the bridge into a single shared helper both `cli.py`/`gateway/run.py` and `run_oneshot()` call (this would also close the 3-dict drift noted in #28892). Per the #61882 precedent, if a non-local backend is configured but cannot be initialized in the oneshot context, oneshot should **fail closed** (error out) rather than fall back to local. Happy to put up a PR along these lines if the approach sounds right.

items.title: [Feature]: Context-Aware Orchestrator Model Routing — Agent self-routes tasks to optimal models

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
## Problem Statement

Hermes Agent currently locks each session to a single model via `config.yaml`. To use different models for different tasks (e.g., a cheap fast model for casual chat, a powerful coding model for implementation work), the user must either:

1. Manually switch models via `/model` slash command every time the context changes
2. Use `delegate_task` subagents, which breaks conversational flow
3. Run separate profiles for different use cases

This makes Hermes a single-model agent rather than an **intelligent orchestration layer** that can route tasks to the best model for the job automatically.

When a user asks "What is the weather today?" vs "Write a React component with TypeScript", the same model processes both — wasting cost on simple queries and potentially underperforming on complex ones.

---

## Proposed Solution

### Core Concept: Agent Self-Routing

The primary agent (not a subagent, not a manual command) should be able to **self-identify the nature of each user request** and route it to the most suitable model automatically — all within the same conversational session.

The routing is:
- **Transparent** — the user just asks, the agent picks the right tool (model) for the job
- **Contextual** — based on the actual content of the conversation, not predefined task types
- **Stateless** — each model swap is clean; tool calls, history, and agent state remain coherent

### Configuration Example

```yaml
model_routing:
  enabled: true
  default: deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash  # fallback for everything else
  routes:
    - match: ["coding", "implementation", "code_review", "debugging"]
      model: qwen/qwen3-235b-a75b
    - match: ["planning", "architecture", "analysis"]
      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4
    - match: ["vision", "screenshot", "ui_analysis"]
      model: nvidia/nemotron-nano-12b-v2-vl
    - match: ["chat", "casual", "quick_answer"]
      model: meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free
```

### How It Works

1. **Detection**: The agent's system prompt includes a routing map. At the start of each turn, the agent analyzes the user's message + recent context and determines the task category (coding, chat, planning, vision, etc.)
2. **Routing**: If the detected category differs from the current model, the agent issues an internal routing request. The framework handles the model swap transparently and continues within the same conversation
3. **Continuity**: Message history, tool call results, and agent state persist across model switches. The user sees a seamless experience
4. **Fallback**: If no route matches, or if the routed model fails, fall back to the default model

### Detection Approaches

**Option A — Agent self-identifies (preferred)**  
The agent's system prompt includes the routing rules and is instructed to classify each incoming message. This is the most flexible approach — the agent understands subtle context.

**Option B — Lightweight classifier**  
A small, fast classification model pre-classifies the message before passing it to the main agent. The classifier itself routes to the appropriate model.

**Option C — Hybrid**  
Agent classifies, but has a `route_task(category)` internal tool as a fallback for explicit routing.

---

## Use Cases

| Scenario | Current UX | With Routing |
|:---|---:|:---|
| Morning briefing + code review in same session | Manually /model switch twice | Agent auto-routes: briefing to fast model, code to coding model |
| Casual chat to suddenly debugging | Stick with expensive model or switch manually | Agent detects debugging context, routes to coding model automatically |
| Multi-step planning + implementation | Suboptimal single model for both phases | Planning to reasoning model, Implementation to coding model |
| Vision task mid-conversation | Cannot use without separate profile | Agent detects image input, routes to vision-capable model |

---

## Relationship to Existing Issues

This proposal differs from:

- **#4461 (Multimodel Routing for Profiles)**: That proposal focuses on predefined static task-category to model mapping in config. This proposal adds **agent self-awareness** — the agent dynamically classifies and routes based on conversation context.
- **#5508 (Per-skill model routing)**: Skill-level routing only works when `delegate_task(skill=...)` is called. The main agent remains single-model. This proposal makes the **main agent itself multi-model**.
- **#38954 (Role-Based Routing)**: Focuses on a fixed planning to coding to review pipeline. This proposal is freeform — any task type, any time, based on actual user input.
- **#157 (Capability Categories)**: More about tool-level model requests. This proposal is about the **orchestrator** (the agent) making routing decisions.

---

## Impact

- **Backward compatible** — when `model_routing.enabled: false` (default), behavior is identical to today
- **Zero user friction** — works out of the box once configured; no slash commands, no manual switches
- **Cost efficient** — cheap models for simple queries, powerful models only when needed
- **Future-proof** — new models can be added to routes without changing agent behavior

---

## Suggested Scope

This is a **medium-to-large feature** requiring changes in:
- `config.yaml` schema (new `model_routing` block)
- Agent runtime (`run_agent.py` or a new `model_router.py` module)
- System prompt builder (inject routing rules)
- Context management (clean model swaps)

However, the core logic is conceptually simple: classify → route → continue.

items.title: Windows: agent turn hangs forever in the git workspace probe when the 2.5s timeout fires (post-kill communicate deadlock)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## What happens

On Windows, when the git probe in `agent/coding_context.py` (`_git`, called from `build_coding_workspace_block`) hits its 2.5s timeout, the whole agent turn hangs forever. The prompt is received, `agent.turn_context` logs the turn start, and then nothing — no model call, no updates, no error. From the outside it looks like the model is thinking indefinitely.

Hit this while driving `hermes acp` (0.18.2) embedded in another app on Windows 11, with the process cwd inside a large git repo (git status legitimately exceeds 2.5s there).

## py-spy stack of the wedged turn

```
Thread "acp-agent_0"
    _wait_for_tstate_lock (threading.py:1139)
    join (threading.py:1119)
    _communicate (subprocess.py:1628)
    communicate (subprocess.py:1209)
    run (subprocess.py:559)          <- TimeoutExpired handler's cleanup communicate()
    _git (agent/coding_context.py:694)
    build_coding_workspace_block (agent/coding_context.py:858)
    ...
    build_turn_context -> run_conversation -> acp_adapter/server.py:1513
```

git itself was already dead at this point (no git child under the process tree).

## Why

`subprocess.run()`'s `TimeoutExpired` handler on Windows kills the child and then calls `process.communicate()` **with no timeout** to collect remaining output. That relies on the pipes reaching EOF. If any other process was spawned concurrently by another thread — an MCP server child, another probe — it can inherit duplicates of the pipe handles (the well-known CPython Windows concurrent-Popen inheritance race), so the pipes never EOF even though git is gone, and the reader-thread join blocks forever. An agent host that registers MCP servers at session start and prompts right after makes this race easy to hit: the git probe runs exactly while those long-lived children are starting.

## Repro sketch

Windows 11, cwd = a large git repo (so `git status --porcelain=2 --branch` exceeds `_GIT_TIMEOUT=2.5`), an ACP session with at least one MCP server configured, prompt immediately after `session/new`. In my environment this wedged 5 out of 5 attempts; adding an artificial delay between session creation and the first prompt (letting the MCP children finish starting) made it pass, which is what pointed at the spawn race rather than git itself.

## Fix

Bound the post-kill cleanup instead of relying on pipe EOF — PR incoming: `_git` switched to `Popen` + explicit `communicate(timeout)` + a bounded (1s) post-kill `communicate`, abandoning the pipes after the grace period. Also sets `stdin=DEVNULL` so a git that decides to prompt can't wait on input. Normal-path behavior unchanged.

items.body:
## Bug Description

Running the official install.sh on a Linux host and choosing **camofox** as the browser provider during `hermes setup` crashes with `FileNotFoundError: '/home/<user>/.hermes/hermes-agent'`. The crash happens *after* the installer has deleted a pre-existing source checkout at that path but *before* it has installed hermes via `uv tool install`, leaving the user with no working `hermes` binary at all.

Two related issues:

1. **Path assumption mismatch.** `_run_post_setup` for camofox assumes a source checkout exists at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` (it subprocess-runs something from that directory). The install.sh path installs via `uv tool install`, which does not create that directory — it puts the package under `~/.local/share/uv/tools/`. So the post-setup step always crashes on a uv-based install when camofox is selected.

2. **Uninstall is not crash-safe.** install.sh deletes any pre-existing `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` source checkout *before* the new install succeeds. If anything later in the wizard crashes (as it did here), the user is left with neither the old install nor a new one. `uv tool list` shows nothing; `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` is gone.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a Linux host, have an existing source-based install at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` (git clone + venv + `pip install -e .`).
2. Run `curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash`.
3. Proceed through `hermes setup`. When prompted for browser automation, choose `camofox`.
4. Accept the default server URL (`http://localhost:9377`).

## Expected Behavior

- Camofox post-setup should not depend on a source checkout at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` when hermes was installed via `uv tool install`.
- install.sh should not remove the previous install before the new one is verified working (or should restore on failure).

## Actual Behavior

Traceback (abridged):

```
File ".../hermes_cli/setup.py", line 2198, in setup_tools
File ".../hermes_cli/tools_config.py", line 4086, in tools_command
```

items.title: Codex transport emits an over-length `prompt_cache_key` (>64) → every openai-codex request 400s and silently falls back

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-caching
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break/degrade prompt caching or cache-key stability (invariant)

items.body:
**Repo:** NousResearch/hermes-agent · **Version:** 0.18.2 (commit `2ccfdb2`)
**File:** `agent/transports/codex.py` (`_CodexResponsesTransport.build_kwargs`, ~line 267)

## Summary

On the `openai-codex` provider (ChatGPT/Codex backend, `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`), hermes can send a `prompt_cache_key` longer than 64 characters. The backend rejects any `prompt_cache_key` over 64 chars with **HTTP 400 BadRequestError**, so the codex request fails on *every* turn and hermes silently falls back to the next provider in the fallback chain. Because the failure is masked by the fallback, the primary provider looks "unused" and the true cause only surfaces if/when the fallback itself fails (e.g. OpenRouter credit/quota).

## Root cause

```python
# agent/transports/codex.py, build_kwargs()
cache_key = _content_cache_key(instructions, response_tools) or session_id
if not is_github_responses and not is_xai_responses and cache_key:
    kwargs["prompt_cache_key"] = cache_key
```

`_content_cache_key` returns a short `pck_<sha256[:24]>` when there is static content to hash, but falls back to the **raw `session_id`** otherwise. There is no length guard. When a caller supplies a long `session_id`, it is forwarded verbatim as `prompt_cache_key` and the OpenAI backend 400s.

## Concrete reproduction

Paperclip (`@paperclipai/server`) hands hermes a session id of the form
`paperclip:company:<uuid>:agent:<uuid>` — **97 chars**. Every `openai-codex`
request then fails:

```
agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 1/3) error_type=BadRequestError
  provider=openai-codex base_url=https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex model=gpt-5.6-sol
  summary=HTTP 400: Invalid 'prompt_cache_key': string too long.
          Expected a string with maximum length 64, but got a string with length 97 instead.
agent.chat_completion_helpers: Fallback activated: gpt-5.6-sol → anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 (openrouter)
```

Credentials are valid; the model is accepted; only the `prompt_cache_key` length is the problem. Nothing in the surfaced error points at the primary provider being the cause — it just silently degrades to the fallback.

## Why it matters

- Silent, total loss of the primary provider on any integration that passes a session id longer than 64 chars.
- The symptom only becomes visible when the fallback also fails, which points debugging in the wrong direction (credentials / subscription / the fallback provider).

## Proposed fix

Cap/hash the key to ≤64 chars at the chokepoint. `prompt_cache_key` is a routing hint only (never a correctness boundary — matching the existing code comment), so hashing an over-length key is safe:

```python
cache_key = _content_cache_key(instructions, response_tools) or session_id
if cache_key and len(cache_key) > 64:
    cache_key = f"pck_{hashlib.sha256(cache_key.encode('utf-8', 'replace')).hexdigest()[:24]}"
```

(`hashlib` is already imported in this module.) This defends against any caller regardless of session-id length or format.

## Environment

- hermes-agent 0.18.2 (commit `2ccfdb2`), editable install
- provider `openai-codex`, model `gpt-5.6-sol`, `api_mode=codex_responses`
- macOS (Darwin), Python 3.11, run under the hermes gateway (`hermes_cli.main gateway run`)

items.title: [Bug]: Gateway queued follow-up delivers intentional-silence markers

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Bug description

When a successful gateway turn returns an exact intentional-silence marker such as `[SILENT]` or `NO_REPLY` while another message is queued for the same session, the queued-follow-up fallback can deliver the marker literally before processing the next message.

This is a core gateway delivery-path issue, not a platform-specific adapter or plugin issue.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Enable gateway streaming.
2. Start a turn whose successful agent result and stream content are exactly `[SILENT]`.
3. Queue a second `MessageEvent` for the same session before the first `_run_agent` invocation unwinds.
4. Observe the first turn's marker being sent directly before the queued turn is processed.

A deterministic gateway regression test reproduces this with a fake two-turn agent and the real stream-consumer/queued-message path.

## Expected behavior

The intentional-silence marker remains in the agent result/transcript but is not delivered to the chat. The queued follow-up is then processed normally.

## Actual behavior

The stream consumer suppresses the marker, but the queued-follow-up fallback sends it through `adapter.send()` because final stream delivery was not confirmed.

The relevant log line is:

```text
Queued follow-up for session ...: final stream delivery not confirmed; sending first response before continuing.
```

The user then sees a literal `[SILENT]` message.

## Root cause

`GatewayStreamConsumer._suppress_silence_marker()` correctly leaves `final_response_sent`, `final_content_delivered`, and `already_sent` false because nothing was delivered.

The queued-follow-up branch in `gateway/run.py` interprets that false delivery state as a reason to send the first response directly:

```python
_already_streamed = _stream_confirmed_final_delivery(...)
if first_response and not _already_streamed:
    await adapter.send(..., first_response, ...)
```

That direct-send path runs inside `_run_agent`, before the normal whole-response filter in `_handle_message_with_agent`, so it bypasses `is_intentional_silence_agent_result()`.

The branch currently conflates two different states:

- the response was not delivered and still needs delivery;
- the response was intentionally suppressed and must never be delivered.

## Proposed fix

Apply the existing canonical `is_intentional_silence_agent_result(result, first_response)` predicate in the queued-follow-up branch before delivery-confirmation fallback logic.

If it is an intentional-silence result, skip `adapter.send()` and continue processing the queued message. Do not mutate the result/transcript, mark the response as delivered, or add platform-specific filtering.

This preserves the existing contracts:

- only successful exact whole-response markers are suppressed;
- failed agent results are not hidden;
- substantive prose mentioning `[SILENT]` or `NO_REPLY` is delivered normally;
- all gateway platforms share the same behavior.

## Regression evidence

Without the queue guard, the integration test captures:

```python
['[SILENT]', 'follow-up response']
```

With the guard, the follow-up is delivered and `[SILENT]` is absent.

The prepared regression and the existing whole-response/streaming suites pass: **77 tests passed** on Python 3.11 with the locked `all + dev` dependency set. Ruff, diff checks, and the Windows-footgun checker also pass.

## Related issue

- #55806 reports the same queued fallback resending a response whose real delivery was not represented by the stream consumer. This issue is distinct: the response was intentionally suppressed, so it must not be treated as delivered or retried.

A tested local patch is ready; I can submit it as a focused PR if maintainers would like one.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `0.18.2`
- Also reproduced against `main` at `7cb2d2cd4acf0c452349968ce8d90908e8fb4cd9`
- Gateway platform observed: Telegram group
- Streaming: enabled

items.title: [Bug]: Docker-backed gateway silently drops MEDIA attachments for container-local /workspace paths

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### Bug Description

When the terminal backend is `docker`, the agent writes its artifact inside the sandbox container and then naturally reports the path it wrote to, either as an explicit directive (`MEDIA:/workspace/chart.png`) or as a bare path in the reply text. MEDIA delivery runs in the **gateway process on the host**, where `/workspace/...` does not exist, so `validate_media_delivery_path` fails `resolve(strict=True)` and the attachment is silently dropped. The user sees the reply text ("here you go:") with **no attachment and no error**.

The gateway already knows about this failure mode, `gateway/run.py` prints at startup:

```
WARNING gateway.run: Docker backend is enabled for the messaging gateway but no explicit host-visible output mount ... is configured. This is fine if the model already emits host-visible paths, but MEDIA file delivery can fail for container-local paths like '/workspace/...' or '/output/...'.
```

but there is no mechanism to make container paths deliverable. Prompting the model (via skill instructions) to translate `/workspace/...` into the host path itself is unreliable in practice, in our deployment the model skipped the translation on roughly half of runs even with the instruction spelled out and a helper that prints the exact host path to paste. An instruction is not a mechanism; the boundary should do the translation.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a messaging gateway (Discord in our case) with `terminal.backend: docker` (sandboxed agent, `/workspace` bind-mounted to a host dir).
2. Ask the bot to produce a file, e.g. "draw a diagram and send it as png". The agent writes `/workspace/chart.png` in its container and replies with `MEDIA:/workspace/chart.png`.
3. Watch gateway.log.

### Expected Behavior

The file, which exists on the host at `<host-workspace-mount>/chart.png`, attaches to the reply.

### Actual Behavior

```
WARNING gateway.platforms.base: Skipping unsafe MEDIA directive path: /workspace/chart.png
```

The reply posts with no attachment and no user-visible error, even though the artifact exists on the host under the workspace mount.

### Proposed fix

An opt-in env `MEDIA_WORKSPACE_HOST_ROOT` naming the host directory that backs the container's `/workspace` mount. When set, both delivery routes (`validate_media_delivery_path` for `MEDIA:` directives, `extract_local_files` for bare paths) remap the fixed `/workspace/` prefix onto it. The remapped path is realpath-fenced inside the mount, must exist, and still passes the full delivery validation (denylist / strict-mode allowlist / recency) afterwards, so the remap grants no new reach. Unset ⇒ behaviour unchanged. PR with tests to follow.

items.title: fix(mcp): catch SDK TaskGroup BaseExceptionGroup and reconnect immediately instead of backoff/park
items.body:
## Problem

Streamable‑HTTP MCP servers that experience a transient SSE stream drop (e.g. idle timeout, brief backend blip) trigger a full session teardown, exponential‑backoff reconnect, and tool deregistration — even though the POST request path is still functional.

### Root cause chain

1. The Python MCP SDK (`mcp.client.streamable_http`) runs a background GET SSE stream inside a TaskGroup.
2. When the SSE stream drops (network hiccup, idle timeout, server‑side TCP close), one of the TaskGroup's child tasks raises.
3. The SDK catches ordinary `Exception` inside `handle_get_stream()` and retries (up to 2 attempts), but any unhandled exception — or a `CancelledError` from sibling‑task cancellation — escapes as a `BaseExceptionGroup`.
4. This `BaseExceptionGroup` propagates out of `streamable_http_client()` into `_run_http()`, which exits both the `ClientSession` and `streamable_http_client` context managers.
5. The exception reaches `run()`'s `except Exception` handler, which sets `self.session = None`, increments `_reconnect_retries`, applies exponential backoff (1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s), and on exhaustion *parks* the server for 300s after deregistering all tools.

**Result:** A ~50ms SSE stream glitch causes MCP tools to be unavailable for seconds to minutes, even though the server is perfectly reachable via HTTP POST.

## Location

**`tools/mcp_tool.py`** — `_run_http()` method (both the new and deprecated API branches at lines ~2500 and ~2532).

Currently the inner `async with streamable_http_client(...) / ClientSession(...)` blocks are unwrapped: any exception from the SDK's TaskGroup propagates directly into `run()`'s error‑handling path.

## Fix

Wrap the transport‑layer `async with` blocks inside `_run_http()` with a `try/except BaseExceptionGroup` that catches the SDK's TaskGroup failure and returns `"reconnect"` — the same code path used for OAuth recovery and manual `/mcp` refresh.

```python
# Line ~2500 (new API branch):
try:
    async with streamable_http_client(url, http_client=http_client) as (...):
        async with ClientSession(read_stream, write_stream, ...) as session:
            ...
            reason = await self._wait_for_lifecycle_event()
            if reason == "reconnect":
                logger.info(...)
except BaseExceptionGroup:
    logger.debug(
        "MCP server '%s': SDK transport TaskGroup exited "
        "(will auto-reconnect immediately)", self.name,
    )
    reason = "reconnect"
```

The outer `run()` loop sees `"reconnect"` — resets retry counters, clears `_ready`, and immediately re‑enters `_run_http()` to establish a fresh transport. No backoff, no parking, no tool deregistration.

## Impact

**Medium.** Affects every Streamable‑HTTP MCP server (the most common transport). Without the fix, any SSE‑stream disruption cascades into multi‑minute MCP tool outages. With the fix, the transport self‑heals in under one second and tools never drop off.

## Related

- Python SDK issue #2114 — `ExceptionGroup` wrapping obscures real errors (root cause at SDK level)
- Python SDK PR #2245 — open P1 fix for the SDK's TaskGroup error handling
- Hermes #38488 — permanent‑give‑up bug (same family, fixed independently)

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

`agent/model_metadata.py` keeps a hand-maintained frozenset, `_PROVIDER_PREFIXES`, that `_strip_provider_prefix()` uses to recognise `provider:model` strings before metadata and context-window lookups. Providers that ship as plugins are not in it, so a string like `fireworks:accounts/fireworks/models/foo` (or any user plugin under `$HERMES_HOME/plugins/model-providers/`, e.g. `alibaba-token-plan:qwen3.7-plus`) never strips. The full string then misses cache and models.dev lookups and falls back to default context lengths.

The same file already solves this exact problem for URL reverse-mapping: `_URL_TO_PROVIDER` auto-extends from registered provider profiles right below its static dict. The prefix set just never got the same treatment, so every new provider plugin silently needs a core edit to be recognised in `provider:model` strings, which is the kind of core edit the plugin surface is meant to avoid.

### Proposed Solution

Auto-extend `_PROVIDER_PREFIXES` from registered profiles, mirroring the `_URL_TO_PROVIDER` block: after discovery, add each profile's `name` and `aliases` (lowercased) to the set. The existing `_OLLAMA_TAG_PATTERN` guard already prevents over-stripping of Ollama `model:tag` strings, so behaviour for those is unchanged.

I have this implemented with a test and will open a PR referencing this issue.

### Alternatives Considered

Keep hand-adding names to the frozenset per provider. That is what happens today (#7575 was this same gap for xAI and was fixed by adding `xai`, `grok` and friends by hand), it works for bundled plugins (though several, like `fireworks`, are currently missing) but cannot work for user plugins, which by design never touch this file.

### Feature Type

Developer experience / plugin surface

### Scope

Small. One auto-extend block in `agent/model_metadata.py` plus a test in `tests/agent/test_model_metadata.py`. No behaviour change for anything already in the static set.
